title: Eurocopter Tiger HAP / HAD (pilot)

sources.title: JoyPro cockpit catalog (panels, items and grip functions of the variant)

intro: The Eurocopter Tiger is a European attack helicopter with two MTR390 engines and two crew in tandem. Unlike most attack helicopters, the pilot sits in front and the gunner (who is also the commander) behind; both seats have flight controls and colour screens. The HAP is the French escort version with a 30 mm gun turret, the HAD the upgraded Franco-Spanish version. Its grip switches are not described in public sources, so this guide lists the basic controls of a NATO attack helicopter pilot and describes the panels in general terms; the gunner's seat is not covered.

areas.name: Instrument panel
areas.text: The screens and the standby instrument.

panels.name: Instrument panel
panels.text: Two colour screens in front of the pilot with a standby instrument and the master warning lights.
panels.context: The Tiger was designed with a glass cockpit from the start; flight, engine and mission data are pages on the screens. JoyPro describes the panels in general terms.

controls.name: Multifunction displays
controls.text: Two colour screens (multi-function screens with buttons around their edge). They show the flight instruments, the map, the engines and the mission pages.
controls.context: Instead of dozens of round dials, the crew picks the page each screen shows; one screen can replace another that fails.

controls.name: MFD bezel keys
controls.text: Buttons around the edge of each screen. Each one picks the word printed next to it on the screen, so the same button does different things on different pages.
controls.context: The crew uses them to change pages and options; the page layout is not described in the sources JoyPro uses.

controls.name: Standby flight instrument
controls.text: A small separate instrument that shows the attitude (nose up or down, leaning left or right), the speed and the height. It keeps working when the big screens fail.
controls.context: It is the backup that lets the pilot fly safely to a landing if the main displays go dark.

controls.name: Master warning / caution lights
controls.text: Two big lights: master warning means "danger now", master caution means "something needs your attention". The message on the display says what is wrong.
controls.context: Pressing the light usually acknowledges it, so it is ready to show the next problem.

panels.name: Centre console
panels.text: The keypad for data entry, the weapon control panel and the audio panel below the screens.
panels.context: The pilot sets up the route, the radios and the weapon stations here.

controls.name: Control display unit
controls.text: A keypad with a small screen where the crew types navigation points and radio frequencies, like a small computer keyboard.
controls.context: The crew sets up the route and the radios with it before the flight and changes them in flight. JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

controls.name: Weapon control panel
controls.text: The switches for the weapons: the master arm (the main safety switch for the weapons: nothing fires while it is off) and the choice of the weapon stations.
controls.context: The pilot arms the weapons only near the target and makes them safe before landing. JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

controls.name: Audio control panel
controls.text: Knobs that choose which radios and the intercom (the phone line between the crew members) the pilot hears, and how loud.
controls.context: The gunner behind has his own panel. JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

areas.name: Side and overhead panels
areas.text: Engine, fuel, electrical and light controls.

panels.name: Overhead and side panels
panels.text: The engine, fuel, electrical and lighting controls.
panels.context: They are used mostly for the start-up and the shutdown.

controls.name: Engine control levers and FADEC switches
controls.text: Two levers, one for each of the two MTR390 engines. They give each engine fuel and decide its power setting, from off through idle to the flying position. FADEC switches next to them control the computers that run each engine by themselves.
controls.context: JoyPro's catalog places the two levers on the left console. In flight the FADEC computers govern the engines, so the levers stay in the flying position.

controls.name: Fuel control switches
controls.text: Switches for the fuel pumps and valves: pumps move fuel from the tanks to the engines, valves open or close the fuel lines.
controls.context: The pilot sets them up before the engine start and uses them when a tank or a pump has a problem. JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

controls.name: Electrical power switches
controls.text: Switches for the helicopter's electricity: the battery and the generators. The battery stores electricity for when the engines are off; generators make electricity while the engines run.
controls.context: They are among the first switches the pilot uses when climbing in, because almost every other system needs electricity. JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

controls.name: Lighting switches
controls.text: Switches and knobs for the lights: the outside lights that show other aircraft where the helicopter is, and the lamps that light the instruments inside. The cockpit lights are made to work with night vision goggles (goggles that make the dark visible).
controls.context: The pilot sets them before a night flight so the instruments are readable without dazzling the eyes. JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

areas.name: Cyclic and collective
areas.text: The flight controls the pilot holds.

panels.name: Cyclic grip
panels.text: The stick between the pilot's knees with the radio trigger, the weapon trigger, the trim controls, the autopilot button and the countermeasures button.
panels.context: JoyPro lists the controls a NATO attack helicopter pilot has, because the Tiger's own grip switches are not described in public sources.

controls.name: Cyclic
controls.text: The cyclic is the helicopter's stick between the pilot's knees. It tilts the rotor: forward makes the helicopter fly forward, back slows it down, left and right move it sideways.
controls.context: It is the main flight control together with the collective and the pedals; on most bindings it is the joystick's X and Y axes.

controls.name: Radio / ICS switch
controls.text: A trigger with two steps on the front of the grip. The first step talks on the intercom (the phone line between the crew members); pulled all the way it transmits on the selected radio.
controls.context: Like the button of a walkie-talkie: the voice goes out only while it is held. The intercom panel decides which radio the second step uses.

controls.name: Weapon fire trigger (guarded)
controls.text: Pulling this trigger fires the selected gun or rockets. A guard covers it so it cannot be pulled by accident.
controls.context: It only fires when the master arm switch is on; the pilot aims with the sight or the helmet display first.

controls.name: Trim switch
controls.text: A four-way switch on top of the grip for the trim, small adjustments so the helicopter flies steadily without the pilot holding the stick against a force. Forward trims the nose down, back up, left and right trim the roll. Each click moves the trim a little (beep trim).
controls.context: The pilot trims after every change of speed, so the cyclic stays where it is without effort.

controls.name: Trim release button
controls.text: While this button is held, the trim lets go of the stick, so it moves freely without any spring force. When it is released, the trim holds the new position as the new centre.
controls.context: The pilot presses it to set a new stick position quickly, for example when changing from cruise to hover.

controls.name: Autopilot disengage button
controls.text: Pressing this button switches off the autopilot modes that hold height, heading or speed, so the pilot has the helicopter fully in hand.
controls.context: The pilot uses it to take over at once, for example when the autopilot does something unexpected.

controls.name: Countermeasures dispense button
controls.text: Pressing this button throws out a stored series of flares (hot burning decoys for heat-seeking missiles) and chaff (clouds of metal strips for radar missiles).
controls.context: The dispensers must be armed first; the pilot presses it when a missile warning sounds.

panels.name: Collective
panels.text: The lever at the left of the seat with the light switches and the weapon select switch on its head.
panels.context: The left hand holds it in flight; the weapon select switch lets the pilot change weapons without letting go.

controls.name: Collective
controls.text: The collective is the lever at the left of the pilot's seat. Raising it makes the main rotor blades bite the air harder, so the helicopter climbs; lowering it makes the helicopter sink.
controls.context: More collective needs more engine power; the pilot raises it gently and watches the torque and rotor speed.

controls.name: Landing / search light switch
controls.text: This switch turns the landing light on and off: a strong lamp under the helicopter that lights the ground in front for landing at night.
controls.context: The pilot switches it on for the approach and the landing in the dark, and off again in cruise.

controls.name: Light position switch
controls.text: A four-way switch that aims the searchlight: forward and back swing it out and in, left and right turn it to the side.
controls.context: The pilot points the light at a landing spot or at something on the ground without taking a hand off the controls.

controls.name: Weapon select switch
controls.text: This switch chooses the weapon for the trigger: up the gun, left the rockets, right the missiles, down no weapon (safe).
controls.context: The pilot picks the weapon before an attack and goes back to safe afterwards.
